summary: On 2020-05-02 the DMEVALS user pbeesly, who is simultaneously running a hands-on-keyboard intrusion on scranton.dmevals.local (Sysinternals download, sdelete anti-forensics, persistence, keystroke logging, exfil staging, PsExec to NASHUA with a plaintext password), requested handles to lsass.exe with all-access masks. At 03:05:16-17 on scranton, powershell.exe (PID 0xba0, logon 0x372e81) requested 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe, including 'Read from process memory' and 'Perform virtual memory operation'. At 03:09:29 on nashua, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 0x1e28, logon 0x85aad2, same user SID ...-1107) requested 0x1f3fff on lsass.exe. The 03:01:03 sysmon event 10 shows powershell.exe (PID 3876) accessing lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1000 via a .NET (System.ni.dll) call trace, consistent with Get-Process/process enumeration rather than a dump. No dump file, no procdump/comsvcs/mimikatz/sekurlsa command line, and no 4104 script block referencing lsass or minidump was found, so a completed LSASS dump is not evidenced - but the full-access handle requests by an interactive attacker session are not explainable as normal system behaviour and warrant host triage.
title: pbeesly PowerShell/wsmprovhost opened lsass.exe with full-access masks (0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff) on scranton and nashua

summary: The only SAM object access in the window is on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19:21-03:20:46, where the requesting process is lsass.exe itself (PID 0x2ec) running as SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3e7) against the 'Security Account Manager' object server, with masks 0xf003f (SAM_SERVER) and 0xf07df (SAM_DOMAIN). This is the local SAM service handling its own account database, not an external tool reading the hive. No reg.exe save of SAM/SYSTEM, no hive file writes (.hiv/.dit), no 4663 on SAM/SECURITY object names, and no 4104 script block referencing reg save or hives were observed.
title: SAM_SERVER / SAM_DOMAIN handle requests are lsass-internal SYSTEM activity, not hive dumping

summary: No process creation on any host referenced ntdsutil, vssadmin, diskshadow or ntds, no file-create event targeted ntds or *.dit, and no 4104 script block mentioned ntds/vssadmin/diskshadow. summary: The only T1040-relevant activity in the dataset is two netsh.exe process creations on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z and 03:19:24Z: 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' followed by 'netsh.exe trace stop'. Both were created by SYSTEM (SCRANTON$, logon 0x3E7) with parent process C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service — the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent, a legitimate packet-capture/network-diagnostics service. The capture ran for only ~7 seconds and no ETL file creation at that TEMP path was observed in Sysmon file-create events. No pktmon, windump, tcpdump, rawcap, tshark or Wireshark execution was found in windows.security 4688 or windows.sysmon event 1, no pcap/npcap/winpcap service was installed (7045 services were only Java VM Support Service and PSEXESVC), no capture driver image loads were seen, and no PowerShell script blocks referenced capture tooling. Zeek (non-overlapping window) shows only ordinary enterprise traffic (SSL 8443, SMB 445, DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, WinRM) with no sign of mirrored/sniffed traffic. This is expected cloud-monitoring behaviour, not adversary network sniffing.
title: netsh trace capture on scranton.dmevals.local spawned by Azure Network Watcher agent (benign)
PowerShell Get-Keystrokes keylogger executed on SCRANTON by pbeesly
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (SID ...-1107) ran a PowerShell keylogging session on 2020-05-02 between 03:06:47 and 03:07:49 UTC. A 'Keystroke-Check' function was defined that enumerates running processes to detect AV products (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — classic keylogger anti-analysis. It was then invoked, followed by 'Get-Keystrokes;Start-Sleep -Seconds 15;View-Job -JobName "Keystrokes"', a second View-Job of the Keystrokes job, and Remove-Job -Name "Keystrokes" -Force to clean up. The same session also ran Invoke-ScreenCapture (screenshot loop saving .bmp to Downloads, confirmed by a file-create of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp) and a steganography loader that decoded and IEX'd a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png. This is interactive input capture on a compromised host.

title: Invoke-ScreenCapture GUI/screen capture loop on SCRANTON
summary: In the same pbeesly PowerShell session on scranton.dmevals.local, a function Invoke-ScreenCapture was defined that uses System.Windows.Forms.SystemInformation::VirtualScreen and System.Drawing.Graphics::CopyFromScreen to grab the full virtual screen every 300 seconds and save it as a randomly named .bmp in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads. It was invoked with 'Invoke-ScreenCapture;Start-Sleep -Seconds 3;View-Job -JobName "Screenshot"', and Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp written by powershell.exe at 03:06:00 UTC. Capturing the GUI is how an operator harvests on-screen credentials/input; no fake credential prompt (CredUIPromptForCredentials/Get-Credential) was observed, so this is GUI capture rather than a credential dialog.

title: PowerShell opens LSASS with full-access masks on SCRANTON and NASHUA
summary: Sysmon event 10 shows PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, the same pbeesly session that ran the keylogger) opening lsass.exe (PID 736) on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16 UTC with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — all-access masks used for reading credential memory. Windows Security 4663 corroborates: powershell.exe accessed \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe as pbeesly at 03:05:16. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (the WinRM host for the pbeesly Invoke-Command to NASHUA at 03:09:23) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29. The remaining LSASS access in the window is benign baseline: svchost.exe (289), Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe (15), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13), and CollectGuestLogs.exe/MsMpEng.exe 4663 reads with AccessMask 0x10. The PowerShell/wsmprovhost LSASS handles are consistent with in-memory credential access rather than a hooking DLL, so confidence is medium.

title: Benign LSASS/SAM handle baseline from Azure guest agents and system processes
summary: Most credential-store handle activity in the window is normal platform behaviour. LSASS access is dominated by svchost.exe (289 events), C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.Security.IaaSAntimalware\1.5.5.9\AntimalwareConfig.exe (15) and C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\Telemetry\WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13), all with read-only masks 0x1000/0x1400. Security 4663 on lsass.exe comes from C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe (4) and C:\Program Files\Windows Defender\MsMpEng.exe (1) with AccessMask 0x10, and the 10 SAM handle requests are all from C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe itself as SCRANTON$ with 0xf003f. Registry 'Keyboard' writes are OS keyboard-layout/device-enumeration values by System, smss.exe, winlogon.exe and LogonUI.exe, not keylogger persistence. No service install (7045) or script referencing keylog/hook was found in windows.other.

title: No web portal capture observed
summary: No evidence of web portal credential capture. All 62 zeek HTTP records in the 2020-04-30 window target a single internal address (url.domain 192.168.0.4), and queries for login/signin/password/keylog URLs returned zero hits. On the Windows side, no file writes to \inetpub\, .aspx/.asp/.ashx files, no IIS/w3wp service installs and no 4688 command lines referencing inetpub were found. The zeek window does not overlap the Windows window, so this is a per-dataset negative.

title: No brute-force authentication activity observed; credential theft on SCRANTON instead
summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events, so no brute-force pattern exists. The only authentication anomalies are successful explicit-credential logons (4648) by DMEVALS\pbeesly from scranton.dmevals.local to NASHUA (10.0.1.6) paired with PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, and a single successful NTLM validation (4776, Status 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork.dmevals.local — consistent with PsExec lateral movement using already-known credentials, not password guessing. The credential-access activity in this window is LSASS memory access (T1003.001), which is outside the T1110 family.

title: No password-guessing attempts; only successful explicit-credential logons
summary: No 4625 events exist in windows.security, so there are no repeated failed logons indicating password guessing. The 4648 events on scranton.dmevals.local/nashua.dmevals.local are all successful (pbeesly to NASHUA, and PSEXESVC.exe to localhost), and the single 4776 on newyork.dmevals.local returned Status 0x0 (success). The PowerShell 4104 hits matching 'password'/'credential' are module manifests and DSC resource strings, plus one exfiltration script that hardcodes a credential (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!) for a WebDAV upload — credential use, not guessing.

title: No offline cracking tooling; LSASS was accessed with full access by PowerShell on SCRANTON
summary: No hashcat/john/wordlist command lines exist (sysmon event.code:1 with hash/ntlm/wordlist returned 0), and no 4663/4656 access to SAM/SECURITY/NTDS hive files by a non-lsass process was found — the 10 SAM object accesses on scranton.dmevals.local are all by C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe under the machine account SCRANTON$ (normal SAM service behaviour). However, on scranton.dmevals.local PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, the steganographic loader spawned by control.exe) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, which is the precursor to dumping hashes for offline cracking. No cracking output files (.pot, hash lists) were observed, so cracking itself is not evidenced.

title: No password spraying: zero failed logons across all hosts
summary: windows.security contains no 4625 events at all, so there is no pattern of one password tried against many accounts. Successful logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25, UTICA$ 5, WEC$ 8) and pbeesly (20) over LogonType 3, plus SYSTEM LogonType 5 — normal service/network authentication. The only repeated user-driven authentication is pbeesly's PsExec-driven 4648 logons to NASHUA, all successful.

title: No credential stuffing: no failed authentications or reused-credential failures
summary: No 4625, 4771 or 4740 events were returned in windows.security, so there is no evidence of stolen credential lists being replayed against accounts. The only credential reuse observed is legitimate-looking: pbeesly's explicit credentials used via PsExec to nashua.dmevals.local (4648 with PSEXESVC.exe) and a successful 4776 NTLM validation on newyork.dmevals.local. The hardcoded 'cozy' credential in the SCRANTON exfiltration script was used for an outbound WebDAV mount, not for stuffing against local accounts.

Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) found no evidence of MFA interception. Every credential-provider / biometric / smart-card / Windows Hello DLL loaded (event.code 7) is Microsoft-signed (win.Signed=true, win.Signature='Microsoft Windows'): CredProv2faHelper.dll, ngccredprov.dll, SmartcardCredentialProvider.dll, BioCredProv.dll, wlidcredprov.dll, vaultcli.dll, cryptngc.dll, ngcsvc.dll, vaultsvc.dll. Registry writes under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Authentication\LogonUI were made by C:\windows\system32\LogonUI.exe during a normal interactive logon of DMEVALS\pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local (LastLoggedOnProvider {60B78E88-EAD8-445C-9CFD-0B87F74EA6CD}, the built-in password provider), not by an attacker-installed provider. No 4624 logon used a smart-card/certificate package (only Kerberos, Advapi, User32, NtLmSsp), and no account names referencing smart/mfa/token/otp/cert/vault/ngc appeared in logon events. The 4648 explicit-credential events are PsExec-driven (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local) and normal Windows internals (winlogon.exe for DWM-1/UMFD-*, taskhostw.exe, svchost.exe) using the pbeesly account, i.e. lateral movement with harvested passwords rather than MFA token interception. The 7045 service installs are PSEXESVC and a Java support service, not credential providers. The only PowerShell script block touching credentials (Invoke-Exfil on scranton.dmevals.local) hardcodes a plaintext password ('MyCozyPassw0rd!') for a WebDAV drive - credential use, not MFA interception. LSASS access by PowerShell.exe/wsmprovhost.exe (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) is credential dumping territory (T1003), not T1111.
title: No MFA interception artifacts; credential-provider and smart-card components are stock Microsoft binaries

title: WebDAV/UNC path used by Invoke-Exfil to force NTLM authentication and exfiltrate a 7z archive to 192.168.0.4
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, a PowerShell scriptblock (ScriptBlockId b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, logged 2020-05-02T03:08:02Z, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) defines function Invoke-Exfil. It compresses the user's Downloads into $env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z with password 'lolol', builds a PSCredential for user 'cozy', then maps a drive to the UNC/WebDAV path \\192.168.0.4\webdav via New-PSDrive and copies OfficeSupplies.7z there with Copy-Item. The WebDAV redirector (Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362, DavClnt) then performs the HTTP WebDAV conversation to 192.168.0.4:80 from 10.0.1.4 — OPTIONS, PROPFIND, LOCK, PUT, PROPPATCH on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, with repeated 401 challenges answered and final 201/204 success — i.e. the host is coerced into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV endpoint, the forced-authentication pattern of T1187. The same host also produced a single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2, target pbeesly, workstation 10.0.1.4, source 172.18.39.2) at 2020-05-02T03:20:41Z, the only NTLM logon in the whole security dataset (all other 217 type-3 logons are Kerberos). Supporting context: PowerShell created C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk at 03:04:23Z and later ran 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' (03:21:26Z); PSEXESVC services were installed on nashua.dmevals.local by pbeesly. The zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window, so the WebDAV flows are the network-side record of the same tooling rather than a time-correlated match.

title: Routine SMB client traffic to file server 10.0.0.4 and Explorer-created Recent .lnk files are benign
summary: The remaining T1187 check hits are normal system behaviour. All 66 outbound SMB (445/139) connections in windows.sysmon are generated by process.executable 'System' (the kernel SMB client) under user SYSTEM, going to 10.0.0.4 (26), the link-local address fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 (24) and 10.0.1.6 (16) — ordinary file-server/DFS traffic, not coercion. The two .lnk files under C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\ were created by C:\windows\Explorer.EXE at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, which is Explorer's normal Recent-items behaviour, not a lure. The 5140/5145 share access is limited to SYSVOL, IPC$ and ADMIN$ (domain administration), and the 4663/4656 object types are overwhelmingly registry Keys. The zeek SMB flows (45 to 445, 5 to 139) are likewise plain conn records. Note the only genuinely malicious shortcut is the StartUp hostui.lnk created by PowerShell, reported in the malicious finding.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, process GUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) — the same process launched at 02:58:44 by control.exe with a steganographic loader reading C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-ing the decoded bytes — opened lsass.exe (PID 736) at 03:05:16 with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS). The call trace is only ntdll.dll+KERNELBASE.dll+UNKNOWN, i.e. no signed dump utility in the stack, consistent with in-memory/reflective access rather than a normal AV/EDR scan. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, spawned 03:09:23 by svchost.exe as pbeesly, i.e. a remote PowerShell/WinRM session) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) at 03:09:29 with 0x1f3fff; its call trace runs through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, indicating a PowerShell cmdlet performing the access. Both hosts were being operated by user pbeesly in the same window (PsExec service installs on nashua, Invoke-Exfil/Invoke-ScreenCapture script blocks on scranton). No credential-dump tooling was observed: no 4688 or Sysmon process-create with lsass/procdump/comsvcs/MiniDump/sekurlsa in the command line, no 4104 script block containing lsass/MiniDump/comsvcs, and no 7045 service install of a dump payload. The remaining LSASS opens are benign baseline (svchost.exe 286x at 0x1000, Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe at 0x1000/0x1400, and wininit/csrss/services at boot 03:19:09). Assessment: suspicious — LSASS was accessed with full rights by attacker-controlled PowerShell on two hosts, but the retrieved data does not show the dump/credential-extraction step itself.
